why_angle: The cited RTINGS, SoundGuys and Vaagame results quote battery ratings and retailer prices, but none divides today's maker price by the rated hours or turns the rating into 3-hour evenings per charge. This page does both for seven headsets. That also shows the four big-brand picks shoppers see cost more than $50 at the makers' stores, and that the cheapest per-hour figure depends on keeping the lights off.

page.after:
What the differences mean

Each figure is the maker's US store price on 2026-11-08 divided by the maker's battery rating. An evening means three hours of play.

  • EKSA E900 BT: $49.99 ÷ 50 h = $1.00 per hour; 50 ÷ 3 = 16.7 evenings per charge. It's the only headset here that costs $50 or less at its maker and has 2.4 GHz, Bluetooth and a 3.5 mm cable. {buy:eksa-e900-bt}
  • EKSA E1000 WT: $35.99 ÷ 36 h = $1.00 per hour; 36 ÷ 3 = 12 evenings. EKSA says a 10-minute USB-C charge adds 3 hours, so 10 minutes on the cable covers one evening. It has only the 2.4 GHz dongle: no Bluetooth and no cable. {buy:eksa-e1000-wt}
  • EKSA E900WT: $39.99 ÷ 80 h = $0.50 per hour with the lights off. With the LEDs on it's $39.99 ÷ 30 h = $1.33 per hour, because the LEDs cut the rating to 30 ÷ 80 = 37.5% of the headline figure.
  • HyperX Cloud Jet: $79.99 ÷ 25 h = $3.20 per hour as rated. SoundGuys measured 19 h 37 min, so $79.99 ÷ 19.6 h = $4.08 per hour.
  • Logitech G321: $54.99 ÷ 20 h = $2.75 per hour, and $4.99 over the budget even on sale.
  • Logitech G435: $79.99 ÷ 18 h = $4.44 per hour. That's 4.4 times the E900 BT's cost per rated hour, but at 165 g it's the lightest headset here.

The EKSA Mako BT is $39.99 with the same three connections: 2.4 GHz (under 30 ms, per EKSA), Bluetooth 5.3 and a 3.5 mm cable. It also has a detachable mic, and EKSA sells a replacement dongle for $9.99. EKSA's store doesn't list its battery hours, so it isn't in the per-hour table. {buy:eksa-mako-bt}

What each battery rating actually measures

A price per hour only compares fairly when the hours are measured the same way, and these makers don't all measure them the same way:

  • Lights off: EKSA rates the E900WT and E1000 WT with their LEDs off. The E900WT drops from 80 h to 30 h with the LEDs on.
  • Split by mode: Corsair gives the HS55 Wireless 24 h on the 2.4 GHz dongle and 37 h on Bluetooth. You'll use the dongle for games, and it lasts 24 ÷ 37 = 65% as long. The table uses the dongle figure.
  • No condition stated: Logitech's G435 (18 h) and G321 (20+ h) pages, HyperX's Cloud Jet page (up to 25 h) and EKSA's E900 BT page (50 h) give no volume, mode or lighting condition.
  • Measured by a reviewer: SoundGuys ran the Cloud Jet for 19 h 37 min on its 2.4 GHz dongle at about 50% volume, 19.6 ÷ 25 = 78% of HyperX's rating. SoundGuys reported the G435 at over 24 h in its testing, more than Logitech's 18 h.

Xbox is a separate limit. EKSA says neither of the E900WT's wireless modes works with any Xbox. SoundGuys says the Cloud Jet doesn't support Xbox consoles at all. EKSA's E1000 BT and G19 BT pages say Xbox connects only by 3.5 mm cable. The E900 BT comes with that cable. The E1000 WT, G435, Cloud Jet, G321 and HS55 don't come with one.

Not recommended

Logitech G321 LIGHTSPEED. It's sold as a budget wireless headset, but Logitech's own store has it at $54.99 (from $59.99), over a $50 budget. Its 20+ h rating works out to 6.7 evenings per charge, against 16.7 for the $49.99 E900 BT. Logitech lists only PS5, PC and Switch / Switch 2, and it has no cable mode for anything else.
